Chapter 7: The Search for Meaning—Why Did This Happen?
After the chaos faded and the world grew quiet again, a single, heavy question hung in the air. Why? Why would a mother, someone meant to protect, commit something so unimaginable?
Everyone seemed to have a theory. Some folks looked back at her childhood—remembering the icy distance, the strict control that shaped her from the very start. Others wondered if the heartache she faced later on—broken relationships, that constant ache to escape, or a desperate need for attention—could’ve pushed her over the edge. Psychologists talked about personality disorders, narcissism, and how some people just can’t really put themselves in someone else’s shoes.
But if you ask the people who actually knew her, none of those explanations ever felt complete. They remembered her softer moments, times she showed real kindness and vulnerability. How could that exist alongside something so dark?
There was a counselor who worked with families in crisis, and she shared something that sticks with you. She’d seen how pain can twist the way a person sees the world—how sometimes, parents get so lost in their own struggles that they forget their children are separate, feeling people. The line between love and harm, she said, is thinner than most of us want to believe. Almost everyone stays safely on the right side of it, but for a few, the weight of old wounds and life’s pressures just becomes too much.
For the children left behind, searching for meaning was even more personal. They wondered, deep down, if they’d done something wrong—if there was anything they could’ve changed. Therapists worked gently, over weeks and months, helping them understand that none of this was their fault. Healing, it turns out, isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about learning how to live with the questions.
The whole town felt the need to make sense of it all, too. Some people leaned on their faith. Others found comfort in sticking to their daily routines. And, as time passed, the story shifted. It became less about the crime itself, and more about how everyone responded—the strangers who showed up with kindness, the professionals who never gave up, and the remarkable resilience of the children.
So, in the end, the search for meaning wasn’t about justifying the tragedy. It was about finding a way to move forward—step by tiny step.
